paras: The attempted lynching of George Simpson took place on the night of September 20, 1888, when a crowd of about eighty Black men went to the jail at Fayetteville, West Virginia, and demanded Simpson, a Black prisoner accused of an indecent assault on a white woman. The sheriff had already sent Simpson into the woods with a deputy, and the next morning he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to three years in the penitentiary. Papers in West Virginia and Virginia carried the story under headlines such as "May be a Lynching" and "Ready for the Lynchers."

According to a Charleston dispatch, Simpson was accused of attempting an indecent assault on "a respectable married white lady" near Echo on the previous Friday and of having "failed in his purpose." He was then lodged in the jail at Fayetteville.

On Thursday night, September 20, a crowd of "eighty colored men" went to the jail, surrounded it, and demanded the prisoner. The sheriff, warned in time, had already sent Simpson to the woods in the charge of a deputy, so the crowd did not reach him. No violence at the jail was reported, and the dispatch did not say what the men intended to do with the prisoner.

Simpson was brought before the court on the morning of September 21, pleaded guilty, and received a sentence of three years in the penitentiary. The crowd was expected to return that night, and the Richmond Dispatch reported that "every precaution" was being taken for his safety. No report of a second visit, of arrests among the crowd, or of Simpson's later fate appears in the coverage.

All of the coverage came from a single Charleston dispatch, printed on September 22 as a special telegram in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer and the Richmond Dispatch and as an unheaded brief in the Alexandria Gazette's "News of the Day." The headlines framed the crowd as would-be lynchers: the Intelligencer used "May be a Lynching," while the Richmond Dispatch called Simpson a "Negro Fiend" in its heading. Each version stated the assault charge as fact rather than as an accusation.

A version dated September 22 ran in the Wheeling Sunday Register the next day as "Ready for the Lynchers," and the Wheeling Register reprinted it verbatim on September 24. That version gave the crowd as "Eight colored men" and said Simpson had been jailed "last night."

Three versions put the crowd at eighty men, while the Wheeling Register version gave eight, apparently from the same text. The September 22 version also implied that the jailing, the crowd and the hearing each happened a day later than the other versions place them; the Alexandria Gazette's "Thursday night" supports the earlier date.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of George Simpson
bases: A crowd of men went to the jail holding an accused Black prisoner and demanded him, and the headlines framed them as would-be lynchers; no one was killed (A1, A2, A4).

No one was killed: the sheriff moved Simpson to the woods before the crowd of 'eighty colored men' reached him, and he was sentenced in court the next morning (A1, A2, A3); the episode is an attempted lynching at most.
Every report is a version of one Charleston, W. Va., dispatch (A1, A2, A3, A4), with A5 a verbatim reprint; no independent local account was found.

accounts.label: Charleston dispatch, Sept. 21
accounts.gist: Eighty colored men went to the Fayetteville jail and demanded Simpson the night before; the sheriff had sent him to the woods; he pleaded guilty that morning and got three years; the mob was expected again.

accounts.label: Charleston dispatch, Sept. 22 version
accounts.gist: Same story, but Simpson was 'caught and jailed at Fayetteville last night' and 'Eight colored men' went to the jail.

framing.detail: The Wheeling Intelligencer headed the dispatch 'May be a Lynching' and stated the assault charge as fact.
The Richmond Dispatch headed it 'After a Negro Fiend' and added that every precaution was being taken for his safety.
The Alexandria Gazette ran it without a headline among the 'News of the Day' briefs.
The Wheeling Sunday Register and Wheeling Register headed it 'Ready for the Lynchers'.

conflicts.note: The Sept. 22 version otherwise copies the same dispatch; 'Eight' is likely a dropped letter, but the papers differ.

versions.value: Simpson jailed after the Friday incident; crowd came the night of Sept. 20 ('last night' on Sept. 21; 'Thursday night')
Simpson 'caught and jailed at Fayetteville last night' in a dispatch dated Sept. 22, which would put jailing, crowd and hearing a day later

conflicts.note: Three versions agree on Sept. 20-21, and A4 appears to be the same text re-dated a day later; the earlier dating is better supported.
